When he distributed his body at the first Supper, the hour was near in which he was 'stricken, smitten of God, and afflicted.' He was so far from intending at that moment to display the glory of his resurrection. And here, what a door is opened to Marcion, if the body of Christ was seen humble and mortal in one place, and glorious and immortal in another! And yet, if their opinion were well founded, the same thing would happen every day, because they are forced to admit that the body of Christ, which is in itself visible, lurks invisibly under the symbol of bread. And yet those who put out such monstrous teachings, far from being ashamed of the disgrace, attack us with bitter abuse because we will not subscribe to them.

But suppose we grant that the body and blood of Christ are attached to the bread and wine. Then the one must necessarily be severed from the other. For just as the bread is given separately from the cup, so the body, joined to the bread, must be separated from the blood, which is contained in the cup. For since they affirm that the body is in the bread and the blood is in the cup, while the bread and the wine are at some distance from each other in space, they cannot by any quibble escape the conclusion that the body must be separated from the blood. Their usual excuse, that the blood is in the body and the body again in the blood, by what they call concomitance, is worse than empty, since the symbols in which they are contained are kept distinct in this way. But if we are carried up to heaven with our eyes and our minds, so that we may there behold Christ in the glory of his kingdom, then, just as the symbols invite us to him in his wholeness, so under the symbol of bread we must feed on his body, and under the symbol of wine drink his blood separately, and in this way have the full enjoyment of him. For though he withdrew his flesh from us and ascended with his body into heaven, he nevertheless sits at the right hand of the Father, that is, he reigns in the power, majesty, and glory of the Father. This kingdom is not limited by any distances of space, nor bounded by any dimensions. Christ can exert his power wherever he pleases, in earth and in heaven. He can make his presence felt by the exercise of his power. He can always be present with his people, breathing his own life into them, living in them, sustaining, strengthening, and reviving them, and keeping them safe, just as if he were with them in the body. In short, he can feed them with his own body, the communion of which he pours into them. In this way the body and blood of Christ are held out to us in the sacrament.

We must hold the presence of Christ in the Supper to be of such a kind that it neither fastens him to the element of bread, nor encloses him within bread, nor confines him in any way; for this would plainly take away from his heavenly glory. And further, it must be of such a kind that it neither strips him of his proper dimensions, nor divides him by differences of place, nor assigns to him a body of boundless extent, spread through heaven and earth. All these things are plainly at odds with his true human nature. Let us never allow ourselves to lose sight of these two limits. First, let there be nothing that takes away from the heavenly glory of Christ. This happens whenever he is brought down under the perishable elements of this world, or fastened to any earthly creatures. Second, let no property be assigned to his body that is inconsistent with his human nature. This is done when his body is either said to be infinite, or made to occupy a number of places at the same time. But once these absurdities are set aside, I gladly admit anything that helps to express the true and substantial communication of the body and blood of the Lord, as it is held out to believers under the sacred symbols of the Supper. We are to understand that they are received not by the imagination or the intellect alone, but are truly enjoyed as the food of eternal life. As for the hatred with which this view is regarded by the world, and the unjust prejudice it incurs when it is defended, there is no cause for it except the dreadful enchantments of Satan. What we teach on this subject is in perfect agreement with Scripture. It contains nothing absurd, obscure, or ambiguous. It is not unfavorable to true godliness and solid edification. In short, there is nothing in it to give offense, except that, for some ages, while the ignorance and barbarism of the sophists ruled in the Church, the clear light and open truth were unworthily suppressed. And yet, because Satan, by means of troublesome spirits, is still in our own day straining to the utmost to bring this teaching into dishonor with every kind of slander and reproach, it is right to assert and defend it with the greatest care.

Before we go any further, we must consider the ordinance itself as Christ instituted it, because the most plausible objection our opponents make is that we abandon his words. To free ourselves from the charge with which they thus burden us, the best course will be to begin with an interpretation of the words. Three of the Gospel writers, along with Paul, relate that our Savior took bread, and after giving thanks, broke it and gave it to his disciples, saying, 'Take, eat: this is my body, which is given,' or 'broken, for you.' Concerning the cup, Matthew and Mark say, 'This is my blood of the new testament, which is shed for many for the remission of sins.' Luke and Paul say, 'This cup is the new testament in my blood.' The defenders of transubstantiation insist that the pronoun 'this' refers to the appearance of bread, because, they say, the whole flow of our Savior's words is an act of consecration, and there is no substance that can be pointed to. But if they hold so strictly to the words, then, since what our Savior gave to his disciples he declared to be his body, nothing is further from the strict meaning of the words than their fiction that what was bread is now body. What Christ takes into his hands and gives to the apostles he declares to be his body; but he had taken bread, and therefore who does not see that what is given is still bread? Hence nothing can be more absurd than to transfer what is said of bread to the appearance of bread. Others, interpreting the word 'is' as equivalent to 'is transubstantiated,' resort to a gloss that is forced and violently twisted. They have no ground, then, for pretending that they are moved by reverence for the words. The use of the word 'is' to mean 'being converted into something else' is unknown to every language and nation. As for those who leave the bread in the Supper, yet affirm that it is the body of Christ, there is great variety among them. Those who speak more moderately, though they press the letter, 'This is my body,' afterward abandon that strictness and remark that it amounts to saying that the body of Christ is with the bread, in the bread, and under the bread. To the reality they affirm we have already referred, and will return at greater length shortly. For now I am only considering the words by which, they say, they are prevented from admitting that the bread is called body because it is a sign of the body. But if they shun everything that looks like a metaphor, why do they leap from Christ's plain pointing to forms of expression that are quite different? For there is a great difference between saying that the bread is the body, and saying that the body is with the bread. But seeing that they cannot maintain the simple statement that the bread is the body, they tried to escape the difficulty by hiding under those forms of expression. Others, who are bolder, do not hesitate to assert that, strictly speaking, the bread is body, and in this way they show that they are truly men of the letter. If it is objected that the bread, then, is Christ, and being Christ, is God, they will deny it, because the words of Christ do not expressly say so. But they gain nothing by their denial, since all agree that the whole Christ is offered to us in the Supper. It is intolerable blasphemy to affirm, without any figure, of a fading and perishable element, that it is Christ. I now ask them whether they hold these two statements to be identical: 'Christ is the Son of God,' and 'Bread is the body of Christ.' If they grant that they are different (and, whether they like it or not, they will be forced to do so), let them tell us where the difference lies. All they can bring forward, I suppose, is that the bread is called body in a sacramental way. From this it follows that the words of Christ are not subject to the ordinary rule, and ought not to be tested by grammar. I ask all these rigid and stubborn enforcers of the letter whether, when Luke and Paul call the cup the testament in the blood, they do not express the same thing as in the earlier clause, when they call the bread the body. There was certainly the same solemnity in the one part of the mystery as in the other, and since brevity is obscure, the fuller sentence better brings out the meaning. As often, then, as they argue from the one expression that the bread is body, I will draw a fitting interpretation from the fuller expression, that it is a testament in the body. What then? Can we look for surer or more faithful interpreters than Luke and Paul? I have no intention, however, of detracting in any way from the communication of the body of Christ, which I have already acknowledged. I only meant to expose the foolish stubbornness with which they wage a war of words. The bread I understand, on the authority of Luke and Paul, to be the body of Christ, because it is a covenant in the body. If they dispute this, their quarrel is not with me but with the Spirit of God. However often they may repeat that reverence for the words of Christ will not let them give a figurative interpretation to what is spoken plainly, that excuse cannot justify them in rejecting all the contrary arguments we bring forward. Meanwhile, as I have already observed, it is right to attend to the force of what is meant by a testament in the body and blood of Christ. The covenant, ratified by the sacrifice of death, would be of no benefit to us without the addition of that secret communication by which we are made one with Christ.

It remains, then, to hold that, because of the close relation the things signified have with their signs, the name of the thing itself is given to the sign, figuratively indeed, yet very fittingly. I say nothing of allegories and parables, lest anyone allege that I am looking for escape routes and slipping away from the present question. I say that the expression Scripture uniformly uses, whenever the sacred mysteries are spoken of, is by way of metonymy, where the name of one thing stands for another closely related to it. For you cannot otherwise understand the statements that circumcision is a 'covenant,' that the lamb is the Lord's 'passover,' that the sacrifices of the law are expiations, that the rock from which the water flowed in the wilderness was Christ, unless you interpret them by such a figure.
[References: Genesis 17:10; Exodus 12:11; Exodus 17:6; 1 Corinthians 10:4; Exodus 3:2; Psalm 84:8; Psalm 42:3; Matthew 3:16.]
[The French edition adds: Certainly, unless we would do away with all reason, we cannot say that what is common to all the sacraments does not belong also to the Supper.]

Should some peevish person, shutting his eyes to everything else, insist on the expression 'This is,' as setting this mystery apart from all others, the answer is easy. They say that the verb 'is' is so emphatic that it leaves no room for interpretation. Even if I were to grant this, I answer that the same verb occurs in the words of Paul, where he calls the bread the communion of the body of Christ. But communion is something different from the body itself. Indeed, when the sacraments are spoken of, the same word occurs: 'My covenant shall be in your flesh for an everlasting covenant.' 'This is the ordinance of the passover.' To say no more, when Paul declares that the rock was Christ, why should the verb 'was' in that passage be thought any less emphatic than in the words of Christ? When John says, 'The Holy Ghost was not yet given, because that Jesus was not yet glorified,' I should like to know what force the verb has there. If our opponents' rule were strictly observed, the eternal being of the Spirit would be destroyed, as if he had only begun to exist after the ascension of Christ. Let them tell me, finally, what is meant by Paul's declaration that baptism is 'the washing of regeneration, and renewing of the Holy Ghost,' though it is certain that to many it was of no use at all. But they cannot be more effectively refuted than by Paul's saying that the Church is Christ. For after introducing the comparison of the human body, he adds, 'So also is Christ,' where he means not the only-begotten Son of God in himself, but in his members. I think I have now gained at least this much, that all people of sense and honesty will be disgusted with the slanders of our enemies, when they give out that we discredit the words of Christ, even though we embrace those words no less obediently than they do, and weigh them with greater reverence. Indeed, their lazy complacency proves that they do not much care what Christ meant, provided it gives them a shield to defend their stubbornness, while our careful investigation should be proof of the authority we yield to Christ. They spitefully pretend that human reason will not let us believe what Christ uttered with his sacred mouth; but how dishonestly they try to fasten this charge on us, I have already largely shown, and will show still more clearly. Nothing, then, keeps us from believing Christ when he speaks, and from accepting everything to which he gives his assent. The only question here is whether it is unlawful to inquire into the genuine meaning.

Those worthy masters, to show that they are men of the letter, forbid us to deviate in the slightest from the letter. On the contrary, when Scripture calls God 'a man of war,' since I see that the expression would be too harsh if it were not interpreted, I have no doubt that the comparison is drawn from man. And indeed the only pretext that allowed the Anthropomorphites to harass the orthodox Fathers was that they fastened on such expressions as 'The eyes of God see,' 'It came up to his ears,' 'His hand is stretched out,' 'The earth is his footstool,' and cried out that God was being robbed of the body Scripture assigns to him. If this rule were accepted, utter barbarism would bury the whole light of faith. What monstrous absurdities could fanatical men not extract, if they were allowed to press every difficult point in support of their teachings? Their objection, that it is not likely that when Christ was providing special comfort for the apostles in their distress he spoke in riddles or obscurely, actually supports our view. For if it had not occurred to the apostles that the bread was called the body figuratively, as being a symbol of the body, the strangeness of the thing would surely have filled them with confusion. For at this very time, John relates that the slightest difficulties perplexed them. They debate among themselves how Christ is to go to the Father, and, not understanding that his words referred to the heavenly Father, they raise the question of how he is to leave the world until they should see him. How then could they have been so ready to believe what is repugnant to all reason, namely, that Christ was sitting at the table before their eyes, and yet was contained invisibly under the bread? Since they show their agreement by eating this bread without hesitation, it is plain that they understood the words of Christ in the same sense as we do, recognizing what ought not to seem strange when mysteries are spoken of, that the name of the thing signified was transferred to the sign. There was therefore, for the disciples as there is for us, clear and sure comfort, not wrapped up in any riddle. And the only reason certain people reject our interpretation is that they are blinded by a delusion of the devil, so as to bring in the darkness of a riddle instead of the plain interpretation of a fitting figure. Besides, if we insist strictly on the words, our Savior will be made to affirm of the bread something different from what he affirms of the cup. He calls the bread body, and the wine blood. There must then either be a confusion of terms, or there must be a division separating the body from the blood. Indeed, 'This is my body' may be just as truly affirmed of the cup as of the bread, and in turn it may be affirmed that the bread is the blood. [The French adds: I mean, if Jesus Christ is enclosed under each of the two signs.]

This shameful falsehood cannot be completely wiped away without disposing of another charge. They give out that we are so wedded to human reason that we attribute nothing more to the power of God than the order of nature allows and common sense dictates. [The French adds: In reading our writings, it will at once be seen how vile and foul these slanders are.]

They object that they have the word in which the will of God has been openly made known. That is true, if only they will let us keep in the Church the gift of interpretation, which should throw light upon the word. I admit that they have the word, but only as the Anthropomorphites of old had it when they made God bodily, and as Marcion and the Manichees had it when they made the body of Christ heavenly or illusory. They quoted such passages as, 'The first man is of the earth, earthy; the second man is the Lord from heaven,' and, Christ 'made himself of no reputation, and took upon him the form of a servant, and was made in the likeness of men.' But these empty boasters think there is no power of God unless they invent some monster in their own minds, by which the whole order of nature is overturned. This is rather to limit the power of God, to try by our inventions what he is able to do. From this word they have assumed that the body of Christ is visible in heaven, and yet lurks invisible on the earth under countless bits of bread. They will say that this is made necessary so that the body of Christ may be given in the Supper. In other words, because they have chosen to extract a fleshly eating from the words of Christ, carried away by their own prejudice, they have found it necessary to invent this subtlety, which is wholly repugnant to Scripture. So far is it from true that we take anything away from the power of God, that our teaching is the loudest in exalting it. But since they keep charging us with robbing God of his honor, because we reject what, by ordinary understanding, is hard to believe, even though it had been promised by the mouth of Christ, I answer, as I did just now, that in the mysteries of faith we do not consult ordinary understanding, but, with the calm teachableness and gentle spirit that James commends, receive the doctrine that has come from heaven. Where they harmfully go astray, I am confident that we keep a proper moderation. On hearing the words of Christ, 'This is my body,' they imagine a miracle utterly remote from his intention; and when, from this fiction, the grossest absurdities arise, having already, by their reckless haste, tangled themselves in snares, they fling themselves into the abyss of the divine omnipotence, so that in this way they may put out the light of truth. So Augustine, speaking of certain people, says: 'It is strange, when they are caught in their own difficulties, over what precipices they fling themselves, in their fear of the nets of truth.'

But since nothing will be more effective in confirming the faith of the godly than to show them that the doctrine we have set down is drawn from the pure word of God and rests on its authority, I will make this plain with as much brevity as I can. The body with which Christ rose is declared, not by Aristotle but by the Holy Spirit, to be finite, and to be contained in heaven until the last day. I am well aware how confidently our opponents evade the passages quoted to this effect. Whenever Christ says that he will leave the world and go away, they reply that this departure was nothing more than a change of his mortal condition. If that were so, Christ would not have put the Holy Spirit in his place to make up, as they put it, for the lack caused by his absence, since the Spirit does not take his place, nor, on the other hand, does Christ come down from his heavenly glory to take up the condition of a mortal life. Surely the coming of the Spirit and the ascension of Christ are set over against each other, and from this it necessarily follows that Christ dwells with us according to the flesh in the same way as that in which he sends his Spirit. Moreover, he plainly says that he would not always be in the world with his disciples. This saying too they think they cleverly dispose of, as if Christ were denying that he would always be poor and lowly, or subject to the needs of a fading life. But this plainly contradicts the context, since the reference is not to poverty and want, or the wretched condition of earthly life, but to worship and honor. The disciples were displeased with the anointing by Mary, because they thought it a needless and useless expense, close to extravagance, and would therefore have preferred that the price they considered wasted should have been spent on the poor. Christ answers that he will not always be with them to receive such honor. Augustine gives no different explanation, and his words are by no means unclear. When Christ says, 'Me ye have not always,' he was speaking of his bodily presence. With respect to his majesty, with respect to his providence, with respect to his unspeakable and invisible grace, what he said is fulfilled: 'Lo, I am with you always, even unto the end of the world.' But with respect to the flesh that the Word assumed, with respect to that which was born of the Virgin, with respect to that which was seized by the Jews, nailed to the tree, hung on the cross, wrapped in linen cloths, laid in the tomb, and made manifest in the resurrection, 'Me ye have not always.' Why? Because for forty days he conversed with his disciples in bodily presence, and, going out with them, he ascended, while they looked on but did not follow. He is not here, for he sits there, at the right hand of the Father. And yet he is here, for the presence of his majesty has not been withdrawn. So, as regards the presence of his majesty, we have Christ always; while, as regards his bodily presence, it was rightly said, 'Me ye have not always.' In bodily presence the Church had him for a few days; now she holds him by faith, but does not see him with the eye. Here, to note this briefly, Augustine makes him present with us in three ways: in majesty, in providence, and in unspeakable grace. Under this last I include that wonderful communion of his body and blood, provided we understand that it is brought about by the power of the Holy Spirit, and not by that fictitious enclosing of his body under the element, since our Lord declared that he had flesh and bones that could be handled and seen. 'Going away' and 'ascending' indicate, not that he merely had the appearance of one going away and ascending, but that he truly did what the words express. Someone will ask, are we then to assign a particular region of heaven to Christ? I answer with Augustine that this is a curious and needless question, provided we believe that he is in heaven.

Consider this. Does not the very word ascension, repeated so often, imply a removal from one place to another? Our opponents deny it, claiming that by height nothing more is meant than the majesty of his rule. But what was the actual manner of his ascending? Was he not carried upward while the disciples looked on? Do not the Evangelists plainly relate that he was carried into heaven? These clever sophists reply that a cloud came between him and them and took him out of their sight, in order to teach the disciples that he would no longer be visible in the world. As if he ought not rather to have vanished in an instant, to make them believe in his invisible presence! Or as if the cloud should have gathered around him before he moved a step! When he is carried up into the air, and the cloud that comes between shows that he is no longer to be sought on earth, we may safely conclude that his dwelling is now in the heavens, as Paul also affirms when he tells us to look for him from there (Phil. 3:20). For this reason the angels remind the disciples that it is pointless to keep gazing up into heaven, because Jesus, who was taken up, would come in the same way as they had seen him ascend. Here the enemies of sound doctrine think they escape by a clever evasion: that he will come in visible form, even though he never departed from the earth but remained invisible among his people. As if the angels had hinted at a twofold presence, rather than simply making the disciples eyewitnesses of the ascent, so that no doubt would remain! It is as if they had said: by ascending into heaven while you watched, he has asserted his heavenly power. It remains for you to wait patiently until he comes again to judge the world. He has not entered heaven to occupy it alone, but to gather you, and all the godly, along with him.

Since the defenders of this counterfeit teaching are not ashamed to dress it up with the support of the ancient writers, and especially of Augustine, I will explain briefly how wrongheaded the attempt is. Godly and learned men have gathered the relevant passages, and so I am unwilling to argue a case already settled; anyone who wishes may consult their writings. I will not even gather from Augustine what would bear on the matter — namely, that the teaching of those who place the body of Christ in the bread finds no help from passages in Augustine, nor from the authority of Scripture, as is proved here and in sections 29 through 31. There is no ambiguity in what he says in The City of God, Book 16, chapter 27; in his comments on Psalms 26 and 46; and in his Tractates on John, 13, 102, 106, 107, and elsewhere.

Since they place so much confidence in this hiding place of an invisible presence, let us see how well they actually conceal themselves in it. First, they cannot produce a single syllable from Scripture to prove that Christ is invisible. Instead, they take for granted what no sound-minded person will grant: that the body of Christ cannot be given in the Supper unless it is covered with the disguise of bread. But this is the very point in dispute, so it can hardly serve as a first principle. And while they chatter on in this way, they are forced to give Christ two bodies, since, according to them, his body is visible in itself in heaven, yet in the Supper is invisible, by a special arrangement. How well this all hangs together is easily judged, both from other passages of Scripture and from the testimony of Peter. Peter says that the heavens must receive, or contain, Christ until he comes again (Acts 3:21). These men teach that he is in every place, but without form. They say it is unfair to subject a glorified body to the ordinary laws of nature. But this answer drags along with it the deranged dream of Servetus, which all godly minds rightly abhor — that his body was absorbed into his divinity. I do not say this is their opinion; but if it is held to be one of the properties of a glorified body to fill all things in an invisible manner, it is plain that its bodily substance is done away with, and no distinction is left between his Godhead and his human nature. Again, if the body of Christ is so changeable and varied that it appears in one place and is invisible in another, where is anything of the nature of a body, with its proper dimensions? And where is its unity? Far more correct is Tertullian, who argues that the body of Christ was natural and real, because its figure is set before us in the mystery of the Supper as a pledge and assurance of spiritual life (Tertullian, Against Marcion, Book 4). The French adds: for the figure would be false if the thing it represents were not real.

Even granting the absurdity they assert about an invisible presence, it would still be necessary to prove his immensity, without which it is useless to try to enclose Christ under the bread. Unless the body of Christ can be everywhere, without any boundaries of space, it is impossible to believe that he is hidden in the Supper under the bread. And so they have been driven to introduce the monstrous teaching of ubiquity. But Scripture has demonstrated, by strong and clear passages, first, that his body is limited by the dimensions of a human body; and second, that his ascension into heaven made it plain that it is not in all places, but, on passing to a new place, leaves the one it formerly occupied. The promise they appeal to — "I am with you always, even to the end of the world" — is not to be applied to his body. For, in the first place, a perpetual connection with Christ could not exist unless he dwells in us bodily, apart from the use of the Supper. They therefore have no good ground for disputing so bitterly about the words of Christ in order to enclose him under the bread in the Supper. The French adds: seeing that they themselves confess we have him just as fully without the Supper.
The French adds: he made Jesus Christ man insofar as he is God, and God insofar as he is man.

They are greatly mistaken in imagining that there is no presence of the flesh of Christ in the Supper unless it is placed in the bread. In this way they leave nothing for the secret working of the Spirit, who unites Christ himself to us. To them Christ does not seem to be present unless he comes down to us — as though we did not equally gain his presence when he lifts us up to himself. The only question, then, is about the manner. They place Christ in the bread, while we hold it unlawful to drag him down from heaven. Which of the two is more correct, let the reader judge. Only have done with the slander that Christ is shut out from his own Supper if he does not lie hidden under the covering of bread. For since this mystery is heavenly, there is no need to bring Christ down to earth in order that he may be joined to us.

Now, if anyone asks me about the manner of it, I will not be ashamed to confess that it is too high a mystery for my mind to grasp or my words to express; and, to speak more plainly, I feel it rather than understand it. Therefore, in the truth of God, on which I can safely rest, I embrace it here without dispute. He declares that his flesh is the food, and his blood the drink, of my soul; I give my soul to him to be fed with such food. In his sacred Supper he bids me take, eat, and drink his body and blood under the symbols of bread and wine. I have no doubt that he truly gives them, and that I receive them. Only, I reject those absurdities that appear unworthy of the heavenly majesty of Christ and inconsistent with the reality of his human nature, since they must also be at odds with the Word of God. For the Word teaches both that Christ was received into the glory of the heavenly kingdom, so as to be exalted above all the conditions of this world (Luke 24:26), and, no less carefully, ascribes to him the properties belonging to a true human nature. This ought not to seem incredible or contrary to reason (Irenaeus, Book 4, chapter 34); for, as the whole kingdom of Christ is spiritual, so whatever he does in his Church is not to be measured by the wisdom of this world. Or, to use the words of Augustine, this mystery is performed by a man like the others, but in a divine manner; and on earth, but in a heavenly manner. Such, I say, is the bodily presence the nature of the sacrament requires, and which we say is here displayed with such power and effectiveness that it not only gives our minds undoubted assurance of eternal life, but also secures the immortality of our flesh, since our flesh is now made alive by his immortal flesh, and in a manner shines in his immortality. Those who carry themselves beyond this with their exaggerations accomplish nothing by their extravagant claims except to obscure the plain and simple truth. If anyone is still not satisfied, I would have him consider for himself that we are speaking of the sacrament, every part of which ought to have reference to faith. Now, by partaking of his body, as we have explained, we nourish faith no less richly and abundantly than do those who drag Christ himself down from heaven. Still, I freely confess that I reject the mixing or transfusing of the flesh of Christ into our soul that they teach, because it is enough for us that Christ, out of the substance of his flesh, breathes life into our souls — indeed, pours his own life into us — even though the actual flesh of Christ does not enter into us. See Bernard, Sermons on the Song of Songs, 74 and 75; and his treatise On Grace and Free Will.

The same view must be taken of communion, which, according to them, has no existence unless they swallow the flesh of Christ under the bread. But no small insult is offered to the Spirit if we refuse to believe that it is by his incomprehensible working that we share in the body and blood of Christ. Indeed, if the nature of the mystery, as it was handed down to us and known to the ancient Church for four hundred years, had been considered as it deserves, there would have been more than enough to satisfy us, and the door would have been shut against many shameful errors. These errors have kindled fearful conflicts by which the Church, both in ancient times and in our own, has been miserably troubled, as inquisitive men insist on an extravagant manner of presence for which Scripture gives no warrant. And over a matter so foolishly and rashly invented, they keep up an uproar, as if the enclosing of Christ under the bread were, so to speak, the beginning and end of godliness. It was of first importance to know how the body of Christ, once delivered up for us, becomes ours, and how we become partakers of his shed blood, because this is to possess the whole of Christ crucified, so as to enjoy all his blessings. But passing over these matters of such great importance — indeed, neglecting and almost suppressing them — they busy themselves only with this one troublesome question: how is the body of Christ hidden under the bread, or under the appearance of bread? They falsely pretend that everything we teach about spiritual eating is opposed to true and, as they call it, real eating, when in fact we differ only over the manner of eating. According to them this is carnal, since they enclose Christ under the bread; but according to us it is spiritual, since the sacred working of the Spirit is the bond of our union with Christ. No better founded is their other objection — that we attend only to the fruit or effect that believers receive from eating the flesh of Christ. We have already said that Christ himself is the substance of the Supper, and that the effect follows from this: that by the sacrifice of his death our sins are atoned for, by his blood we are washed, and by his resurrection we are raised to the hope of life in heaven. But a foolish notion, of which Lombard was the author, distorts their minds, for they think that the sacrament is the eating of the flesh of Christ. His words are: "The sacrament, and not the thing, is the forms of bread and wine; the sacrament and the thing are the flesh and blood of Christ; the thing and not the sacrament is his mystical flesh" (Lombard, Book 4, Distinction 8). And again, a little later: "The thing signified and contained is the actual flesh of Christ; the thing signified but not contained is his mystical body." To his distinction between the flesh of Christ and the power of nourishing that it possesses, I agree; but his maintaining that it is a sacrament, and a sacrament contained under the bread, is an error not to be tolerated. From this has arisen that false interpretation of sacramental eating, because it was imagined that even the wicked and profane, however far estranged from Christ, eat his body. But the flesh of Christ itself in the mystery of the Supper is no less a spiritual matter than eternal salvation. From this we conclude that all who are devoid of the Spirit of Christ can no more eat the flesh of Christ than they can drink wine that has no taste. Surely Christ is shamefully torn apart when his body, as though lifeless and without any power, is prostituted to unbelievers. This is plainly contrary to his words: "He who eats my flesh and drinks my blood dwells in me, and I in him" (John 6:56). They object that he is not there speaking of sacramental eating. This I grant, provided they will not keep stumbling over this stone — that his flesh itself is eaten without any benefit. I should like to know how they hold it in once they have eaten it. Here, in my judgment, they will find no way out. But they object that the ingratitude of man cannot in any respect detract from, or interfere with, faith in the promises of God. I admit and hold that the power of the sacrament remains whole, however the wicked may labor with all their might to destroy it. Still, it is one thing to be offered, another to be received. Christ gives this spiritual food and holds forth this spiritual drink to all. Some eat eagerly; others contemptuously reject it. Will their rejection cause the food and drink to lose their nature? They will say that this comparison supports their opinion — namely, that the flesh of Christ, though it be without taste, is still flesh. But I deny that it can be eaten without the taste of faith; or, if it is more agreeable to speak with Augustine, I deny that men carry away more from the sacrament than they gather in the vessel of faith. So nothing is taken away from the sacrament; indeed, its reality and effectiveness remain unimpaired, even though the wicked, after partaking of it outwardly, go away empty. If, again, they object that it detracts from the saying "This is my body" if the wicked receive corruptible bread and nothing more, it is easy to answer that God wills his truth to be recognized, not in the bare receiving, but in the constancy of his goodness, since he is ready to perform — indeed, freely offers to the unworthy — what they reject. The integrity of the sacrament, an integrity the whole world cannot violate, lies here: that the flesh and blood of Christ are no less truly given to the unworthy than to the elect believers of God. And yet it is true that, just as rain falling on hard rock runs off because it cannot penetrate, so the wicked, by their hardness, repel the grace of God and keep it from reaching them. We may add that it is no more possible to receive Christ without faith than it is for seed to sprout in fire. They ask how Christ can have come for the condemnation of some unless they unworthily receive him. But this is absurd, since we nowhere read that they bring death upon themselves by receiving Christ unworthily, but by rejecting him. They get no help from the parable in which Christ says that the seed which fell among thorns sprang up but was afterward choked (Matt. 13:7), because there he is speaking of the effect of a temporary faith — a faith that those who place Judas, in this respect, on the same footing as Peter do not think necessary to the eating of the flesh and the drinking of the blood of Christ. Indeed, their error is refuted by that same parable, when Christ says that some seed fell on the path, and some on stony ground, and yet neither took root. From this it follows that the hardness of those who profess belief is an obstacle that keeps Christ from reaching them. All who would have our salvation furthered by this sacrament will find nothing more fitting than to lead believers to the fountain, that they may draw life from the Son of God. Its dignity is amply enough commended when we hold that it is a help by which we may be grafted into the body of Christ, or, being already grafted in, may be more and more united to him, until that union is completed in heaven. They object that Paul could not have made them guilty of the body and blood of the Lord if they had not partaken of them (1 Cor. 11:27). I answer that they were not condemned for having eaten, but only for having profaned the ordinance by trampling underfoot the pledge they ought to have received with reverence — the pledge of sacred union with God.
Moreover, among ancient writers, Augustine especially maintained this. See Augustine, Against the Letters of Petilian, Book 2, chapter 47, and his Tractates on John.

This consideration will easily turn us away from that carnal adoration which some men have, with perverse rashness, introduced into the sacrament, reasoning with themselves in this way: if it is body, then the soul and divinity go along with the body and cannot be separated from it, and therefore Christ must be adored there. First, if we deny their so-called concomitance, what will they do? For, since they chiefly insist on the absurdity of separating the body of Christ from his soul and divinity, what sane and sober man can convince himself that the body of Christ is Christ? They think they fully establish this by their syllogisms. But since Christ speaks separately of his body and his blood, without describing the manner of his presence, how, in a doubtful matter, can they arrive at the certainty they desire? What then? Should their consciences ever be troubled with some weightier dread, will they at once set them free and dissolve those fears by their syllogisms? In other words, when they see that no certainty can be had from the Word of God — in which alone our minds can rest, and apart from which they go astray the very first moment they begin to reason — when they see themselves opposed by the teaching and practice of the apostles, and supported by no authority but their own, how will they feel? To such feelings other sharp stings will be added. What? Was it a small matter to worship God under this form without any express command? In a matter touching the true worship of God, were we to act so casually, without one word of Scripture? Had all their thoughts been kept in due subjection to the Word of God, they would surely have listened to what he himself said — "Take, eat, and drink" — and obeyed the command by which he tells us to receive the sacrament, not to worship it. Those who receive it without adoration, as God commanded, are secure that they do not depart from his command. In undertaking any work, nothing is better than this security. They have the example of the apostles, of whom we do not read that they fell down and worshiped, but that they sat down, took, and ate. They have the practice of the apostolic Church, where, as Luke relates, believers communicated, not in adoration, but in the breaking of bread (Acts 2:42). They have the teaching of the apostles, as Paul taught it to the Corinthian Church, declaring that what he delivered he had received from the Lord (1 Cor. 11:23).

The aim of these remarks is to lead godly readers to reflect how dangerous it is, in matters of such difficulty, to wander from the simple Word of God to the dreams of our own brains. What has been said above should free us from all anxiety in this matter. For the godly soul to truly lay hold of Christ in the sacrament, it must rise to heaven. But if the purpose of the sacrament is to aid the weakness of the human mind, helping it to rise upward so as to perceive the height of spiritual mysteries, then those who stop short at the outward sign stray from the right path of seeking Christ. What then? Can we deny that the worship is superstitious when men fall down before bread in order to worship Christ in it? The Council of Nicaea undoubtedly intended to meet this evil when it forbade us to fix our humble attention on the visible signs. And for no other reason was it formerly the custom, before consecration, to call aloud to the people to lift up their hearts — sursum corda. Scripture itself, too, besides carefully recounting the ascension of Christ, by which he withdrew his bodily presence from our eyes and company so as to make us abandon all carnal thoughts of him, whenever it mentions him directs us to lift up our minds and seek him in heaven, seated at the right hand of the Father (Col. 3:2). According to this rule, we ought rather to have adored him spiritually in the heavenly glory than to have devised that perilous kind of adoration filled with gross and carnal ideas of God. Those, therefore, who devised the adoration of the sacrament not only dreamed it up on their own, without any authority from Scripture, where no mention of it can be shown — for it would not have been left out, had it been pleasing to God — but, disregarding Scripture, they forsook the living God and fabricated a god for themselves after the craving of their own hearts. For what is idolatry, if not to worship the gifts in place of the giver? Here the sin is twofold: the honor robbed from God is transferred to the creature, and God is, moreover, dishonored by the pollution and profaning of his own goodness, while his holy sacrament is turned into a detestable idol. Let us, on the contrary, that we may not fall into the same pit, wholly confine our eyes, ears, hearts, minds, and tongues to the sacred teaching of God. For this is the school of the Holy Spirit, that best of masters, in which such progress is made that, while nothing is to be learned anywhere else, we must willingly be ignorant of whatever is not taught there.

Then, since superstition, once it has crossed its proper bounds, has no end to its errors, men went much further. For they devised rites altogether foreign to the institution of the Supper — and to such a degree that they paid divine honors to the sign. They say their veneration is offered to Christ. First, if this were done within the Supper, I would say that the only legitimate adoration is the one that does not stop at the sign but rises to Christ, seated in heaven. Now, on what pretext do they claim to honor Christ in that bread, when they have no promise of this kind? They consecrate the host, as they call it, carry it about in solemn procession, and formally display it to be admired, reverenced, and invoked. I ask: by what power do they think it is duly consecrated? They will quote the words "This is my body." I, on the contrary, will object that it was said at the same time, "Take, eat." Nor will I treat the other clause as nothing; for I hold that, since the promise is joined to the command, the promise is so included under the command that it cannot possibly be separated from it. This will be made clearer by an example. God gave a command when he said, "Call upon me," and added a promise, "I will deliver you" (Ps. 50:15). If anyone were to call upon Peter or Paul and base it on this promise, would not all cry out that he does so in error? And what else, pray, do those do who, disregarding the command to eat, fasten on the truncated promise "This is my body," in order to twist it toward rites foreign to the institution of Christ? Let us remember, then, that this promise has been given to those who keep the command joined to it, and that those who turn the sacrament to another end have no support from the Word of God. We have already shown how the mystery of the sacred Supper contributes to our faith in God. But since the Lord not only reminds us of this great gift of his goodness, as we explained earlier, but in a manner passes it from hand to hand and presses us to recognize it, he at the same time warns us not to be ungrateful for the kindness thus bestowed, but rather to proclaim it with the praise that is fitting, and to celebrate it with thanksgiving. Accordingly, when he delivered the institution of the sacrament to the apostles, he taught them to do it in remembrance of him — which Paul interprets as "to show forth his death" (1 Cor. 11:26). And this means that all should publicly, and with one mouth, confess that all our confidence of life and salvation is placed in our Lord's death, that we ourselves may glorify him by our confession and, by our example, stir up others also to give him glory. Here, again, we see the aim of the sacrament — namely, to keep us in remembrance of Christ's death. When we are ordered to show forth the Lord's death until he comes again, all that is meant is that we should, with confession of the mouth, proclaim what our faith has recognized in the sacrament — namely, that the death of Christ is our life. This is the second use of the sacrament, and it relates to outward confession.

Third, the Lord intended it to be a kind of exhortation — than which no other could more strongly urge or rouse us — both to purity and holiness of life, and also to charity, peace, and concord. For there the Lord communicates his body to us in such a way that he becomes altogether one with us, and we with him. Moreover, since he has only one body, of which he makes us all partakers, we must necessarily, by this partaking, all become one body. This unity is represented by the bread that is shown in the sacrament. As it is made of many grains, mingled together so that one cannot be distinguished from another, so our minds ought to be so warmly united as to allow no dissension or division. I prefer to give this in the words of Paul: "The cup of blessing which we bless, is it not the communion of the blood of Christ? The bread which we break, is it not the communion of the body of Christ? For we, being many, are one bread and one body, for we are all partakers of that one bread" (1 Cor. 10:16, 17). We shall have profited wonderfully in the sacrament if this thought has been impressed and engraved on our minds: that none of our brothers can be hurt, despised, rejected, injured, or in any way offended without our, at the same time, hurting, despising, and injuring Christ; that we cannot have dissension with our brothers without, at the same time, dissenting from Christ; that we cannot love Christ without loving our brothers; that the same care we take of our own body we ought to take of the body of our brothers, who are members of our body; and that, as no part of our body suffers pain without it spreading to the other parts, so every evil our brother suffers ought to stir our compassion. This is why Augustine, not without good reason, often calls this sacrament the bond of charity. What stronger spur could be used to stir up mutual love than when Christ, presenting himself to us, not only invites us by his example to give and devote ourselves to one another, but, inasmuch as he makes himself common to all, also makes us all to be one in him?

This most admirably confirms what I said elsewhere — namely, that there cannot be a right administration of the Supper without the Word. Whatever benefit we draw from the Supper requires the Word. Whether we are to be strengthened in faith, or trained in confession, or stirred up to our duty, there is need of preaching. Nothing, therefore, can be more absurd than to turn the Supper into a silent action. This is done under the tyranny of the Pope, where the whole effect of consecration is made to depend on the intention of the priest, as if it in no way concerned the people, to whom above all the mystery ought to have been explained. This error has arisen from not observing that those promises by which consecration is effected are intended, not for the elements themselves, but for those who receive them. Christ does not address the bread and tell it to become his body, but bids his disciples eat, and promises them the communion of his body and blood. And, following the order Paul sets down, the promises are to be offered to believers along with the bread and the cup. So indeed it is. We are not to imagine some magical incantation and think it enough to mutter the words, as though the elements heard them; rather, we are to regard those words as a living sermon, meant to build up the hearers, to penetrate their minds, to be impressed and seated in their hearts, and to exert its power in fulfilling what it promises. For these reasons it is clear that the setting apart of the sacrament, which some insist on, so that an extra portion of it may be carried to the sick, is useless. Either they will receive it without hearing the words of institution read, or the minister will join the true explanation of the mystery to the sign. In the silent dispensing of it, there is both abuse and defect. If the promises are recited, and the mystery is expounded, so that those who are to receive may receive it to their benefit, there can be no doubt that this is the true consecration. What, then, becomes of that other consecration, whose effect supposedly reaches even to the sick? But those who do this have the example of the early Church. I admit it; but in a matter of such importance, where error is so dangerous, nothing is safer than to follow the truth.

We see that this sacred bread of the Lord's Supper is spiritual food. To those who worship God in godliness, it is sweet and good to taste, and no less wholesome. When they taste it, they feel that Christ is their life. They are moved to give thanks, and they are stirred up to love one another. But on the other hand, this same bread becomes the most harmful poison to everyone whom it does not nourish and strengthen in faith, and whom it does not move to thanksgiving and love. For just as bodily food, when it enters a stomach already burdened with disease, becomes itself spoiled and corrupted, and harms rather than nourishes, so this spiritual food also, if it is given to a soul polluted with malice and wickedness, plunges that soul into greater ruin. This is not because of any defect in the food, but because, as Scripture says, "to those who are defiled and unbelieving, nothing is pure" (Titus 1:15), however much the food may be sanctified by the Lord's blessing. For as Paul says, "Whoever eats this bread and drinks this cup of the Lord unworthily shall be guilty of the body and blood of the Lord," and "eats and drinks judgment to himself, not discerning the Lord's body" (1 Cor. 11:27, 29).

People of this kind, who without any spark of faith and without any zeal for love rush forward like swine to seize the Lord's Supper, do not at all discern the Lord's body. Since they do not believe that this body is their life, they put every possible insult upon it. They strip it of all its dignity, and they profane and defile it by the way they receive it, because while they are alienated and estranged from their brothers and sisters, they dare to mix the sacred symbol of Christ's body with their quarrels. It is no thanks to them that the body of Christ is not torn to pieces. This is why they are justly held guilty of the body and blood of the Lord, which with sacrilegious irreverence they so vilely pollute.

By eating unworthily in this way, they bring judgment upon themselves. For though they have no faith in Christ, yet by receiving the sacrament they profess to rest their salvation in him alone and to renounce all other confidence. So they become their own accusers; they bear witness against themselves; they seal their own condemnation. And then, divided and cut off from their brothers and sisters by hatred and ill will, that is, cut off from the members of Christ, they have no part in Christ, and yet they declare that the only safety is to share in communion with Christ and be joined to him.

For this reason Paul commands a person to examine himself before he eats of that bread and drinks of that cup (1 Cor. 11:28). By this, as I understand it, he means that each individual should look within himself and consider several things. First, whether with inward confidence of heart he relies on the salvation obtained by Christ, and confesses it with his mouth. Second, whether with zeal for purity and holiness he strives to imitate Christ; whether, following his example, he is ready to give himself to his brothers and sisters, and to hold himself as one in common with those with whom he holds Christ in common; whether, just as he himself is regarded by Christ, he in turn regards all his brothers and sisters as members of his own body, and like his own members desires to cherish, defend, and help them. This is not because the duties of faith and love can now be made perfect in us, but because we ought to strive and seek, with all our heart, to grow daily in our faith.

In trying to prepare people to eat worthily, men have often dreadfully troubled and tortured wretched consciences, and yet have not reached their goal at all. They have said that those who are in a state of grace eat worthily. And being in a state of grace they have taken to mean being pure and free from all sin. By this definition, every person who ever has been or now is upon the earth would be shut out from the use of this sacrament. For if we are to seek our worthiness in ourselves, it is all over with us; nothing awaits us but despair and deadly ruin. Though we struggle to the utmost, we will not only make no progress, but we will be most unworthy at the very moment we have labored hardest to make ourselves worthy.

To heal this sore, they devised a way of obtaining worthiness, namely, that after we have examined ourselves as far as we can and taken account of all our actions, we are to make up for our unworthiness by contrition, confession, and satisfaction. I have spoken of the true nature of this kind of expiation in its proper place (Book 3, chapter 4, sections 2, 17, 27). As far as our present subject is concerned, I say that such things give poor and fleeting comfort to alarmed and downcast consciences that are struck with terror at their sins. For if the Lord, by his prohibition, admits no one to share in his Supper except the righteous and the innocent, every person would need to be cautious before feeling secure of that righteousness of his own which he is told God requires. But how are we to be assured that those who have done what was in their power have fulfilled their duty to God? Even if we were assured of this, who would dare to assure himself that he had done what lay within him? So, since there is no sure security for our worthiness, access to the Supper would always be barred by the dreadful sentence, "He who eats and drinks unworthily eats and drinks judgment to himself."

It is now easy to judge what the nature of this teaching is, and who its author is, the teaching that prevails in the papacy, which by its inhuman harshness deprives and robs wretched sinners, weighed down with sorrow and trembling, of the comfort of this sacrament, a sacrament in which all that is delightful in the gospel was set before them. Surely the devil could have no quicker way of destroying people than by deceiving them in this manner, and so shutting them out from the taste and savor of this food with which their most merciful Father in heaven was pleased to feed them. Therefore, so that we may not plunge over such a cliff, let us remember that this sacred feast is medicine for the sick, comfort for the sinner, and generosity for the poor; while to the healthy, the righteous, and the rich, if any such could be found, it would be of no value at all.

For while Christ is given to us there for food, we recognize that without him we fail, waste away, and perish, just as hunger destroys the strength of the body. And since he is given for life, we recognize that without him we are certainly dead. Therefore the best and only worthiness we can bring to God is to offer him our own vileness and, if I may put it this way, our unworthiness, so that his mercy may make us worthy; to despair of ourselves, so that we may be comforted in him; to humble ourselves, so that we may be lifted up by him; to accuse ourselves, so that we may be justified by him; and moreover to aspire to that unity which he commends to us in the Supper, so that, as he makes us all one in himself, we may desire to have all one soul, one heart, one tongue.

If we weigh and meditate on these things, we may be shaken, but we will never be overwhelmed by thoughts such as these: How shall we, who are devoid of all good, polluted by the defilements of sin, and half dead, worthily eat the body of the Lord? We shall instead consider that we, who are poor, are coming to a generous giver; sick, to a physician; sinful, to the author of righteousness; in short, dead, to him who gives life. We shall consider that the worthiness which God commands consists especially in faith, which places all things in Christ and nothing in ourselves, and in love, a love which, even though it is imperfect, it may be enough to offer to God, so that he may increase it, since it cannot be fully rendered.

Some, who agree with us in holding that worthiness consists in faith and love, have nevertheless gone badly astray about the measure of that worthiness. They demand a perfection of faith to which nothing can be added, and a love equal to the love Christ showed toward us. And in this way, just like the other group, they shut out all people from access to this sacred feast. For if their view were well founded, everyone who receives would receive unworthily, since all, without exception, are guilty and chargeable with imperfection. And surely it would be too foolish, not to say senseless, to require for the receiving of the sacrament a perfection that would make the sacrament empty and unnecessary. For the sacrament was not instituted for the perfect, but for the weak and feeble, to stir up, awaken, urge on, and exercise the feeling of faith and love, and at the same time to correct the deficiency of both.

As for the outward form of the ordinance, it makes no difference whether or not believers take the bread into their hands and divide it among themselves, or each eats what is given to him; whether they return the cup to the deacon or hand it to their neighbor; whether the bread is leavened or unleavened, and the wine red or white. These things are indifferent, and are left free to the Church, although it is certain that it was the custom of the ancient Church for all to receive into their hand. And Christ said, "Take this and divide it among yourselves" (Luke 22:17). History tells us that leavened, ordinary bread was used until the time of Alexander, the bishop of Rome, who was the first to take pleasure in unleavened bread. I cannot see for what reason, unless it was to draw the wondering eyes of the people by the novelty of the spectacle, rather than to train them in sound religion. I appeal to all who have the least zeal for godliness: do they not plainly perceive both how much more brightly the glory of God is displayed here, and how much more abundant spiritual comfort is felt by believers, than in these stiff and theatrical follies, which have no other use than to impress the gaping crowd? They call it restraining the people by religion, when in fact the people, dazed and bewildered, are dragged this way and that by superstition.

Should anyone choose to defend such inventions by their age, I am well aware how ancient is the use of chrism and exorcism in baptism, and how, not long after the age of the apostles, the Supper was corrupted by adulteration. Such, indeed, is the boldness of human presumption, which cannot hold itself in check, but is always toying and trifling with the mysteries of God. But let us remember that God sets such value on obedience to his Word that by it he would have us judge his angels and the whole world.

If all this mass of ceremonies were set aside, the sacrament could be celebrated in the most fitting way, if it were given to the Church very often, at least once a week. It should begin with public prayer. Next, a sermon should be preached. Then the minister, having placed bread and wine on the table, should read the institution of the Supper. He should then explain the promises that are given in it, and at the same time keep back from communion all those who are barred by the prohibition of the Lord. Afterward he should pray that the Lord, with the same kindness with which he has bestowed this sacred food upon us, would also shape and instruct us to receive it with faith and gratitude, and that, since we are of ourselves unworthy, he would by his mercy make us worthy of the feast. Here either a psalm should be sung, or something read, while the faithful, in order, share in the sacred feast, the minister breaking the bread and giving it to the people. When the Supper is ended, an exhortation should be given to sincere faith and confession of faith, to love, and to lives befitting Christians. Lastly, thanks should be offered, and the praises of God should be sung. When this is done, the church should be dismissed in peace.

What we have said so far about the sacrament shows abundantly that it was not instituted to be received once a year, and that carelessly (as is now commonly the custom), but so that all Christians might have it in frequent use, and might often call to mind the sufferings of Christ, thereby supporting and strengthening their faith. By it they stir themselves up to sing the praises of God and to proclaim his goodness; and they cherish and demonstrate toward one another that mutual love whose bond they see in the unity of the body of Christ. As often as we share in the symbol of our Savior's body, as if a pledge were given and received, we bind ourselves to one another in all the duties of love, so that none of us may do anything to offend a brother or sister, or fail to do anything by which we can help them when necessity demands and opportunity allows.

That this was the practice of the apostolic Church, Luke informs us in the Acts, when he says that "they continued steadfastly in the apostles' teaching and fellowship, and in the breaking of bread, and in prayers" (Acts 2:42). So we ought always to make sure that no meeting of the Church is held without the Word, prayer, the dispensing of the Supper, and almsgiving. We can gather from Paul that this was the order observed by the Corinthians, and it is certain that this was the practice for many ages afterward. So, by the ancient canons that are attributed to Anacletus and Calixtus, after the consecration was made, all were to share in communion who did not wish to be outside the bounds of the Church. And in those ancient canons that bear the name Apostolic, it is said that those who do not stay to the end, and do not partake of the sacred communion, are to be corrected, as causing disturbance to the Church. In the Council of Antioch it was decreed that those who come into the church, hear the Scriptures, and abstain from communion are to be removed from the Church until they amend their fault. And although in the first Council of Toulouse this was softened, or at least stated in milder terms, yet there too it was decreed that those who, after hearing the sermon, never communicated were to be admonished, and if they still abstained after admonition, they were to be excluded.

By these decrees, holy men wished to keep and ensure the practice of frequent communion, as it had been handed down by the apostles themselves. They saw that this practice, while it was most beneficial to believers, was gradually falling out of use through the negligence of the people. Of his own age, Augustine testifies: "The sacrament of the unity of our Lord's body is, in some places, provided daily, and in others at certain intervals, at the Lord's table; and at that table some partake to life, and others to destruction" (Augustine, Tractate 26 on John 6). And in his first letter to Januarius he says: "Some communicate daily in the body and blood of the Lord; others receive it on certain days. In some places, not a day passes on which it is not offered; in others, it is offered only on the Sabbath and the Lord's day; in others, on the Lord's day only."

But since, as we have said, the people were sometimes negligent, holy men pressed them with severe rebukes, so that they might not seem to wink at their laziness. We have an example of this in Chrysostom, on the letter to the Ephesians (Homily 26). "It was not said to the man who dishonored the feast, 'Why have you not taken your seat?' but 'How did you come in?' (Mt. 22:12). Whoever does not partake of the sacred rites is wicked and shameless in being present. Suppose someone who was invited to a feast were to come in, wash his hands, take his seat, and seem to prepare to eat, and then taste nothing. Would he not, I ask, insult both the feast and the host? So you, standing among those who prepare themselves by prayer to receive the sacred food, profess to be one of their number by the mere fact that you do not leave, and yet you do not partake. Would it not have been better not to have shown up at all? You say, 'I am unworthy.' Then neither were you worthy of the communion of prayer, which is the preparation for receiving the sacred mystery."

Most certainly, the custom that prescribes communion once a year is an invention of the devil, by whatever means it may have been introduced. They say that Zephyrinus was the author of the decree, though it is not possible to believe that it was the same as we now have it. It may be that, given the times then, he did not, by his ordinance, advise badly for the Church. For there can be no doubt that at that time the sacred Supper was given to the faithful at every meeting, and there can be no doubt that a great many of them communicated. But since it almost never happened that all could communicate at the same time, and since it was necessary that those who were mixed among the profane and the idolaters should testify to their faith by some external symbol, this holy man, with a view to order and government, appointed that day, so that on it the whole of Christendom might give a confession of their faith by sharing in the Lord's Supper.

The ordinance of Zephyrinus, which was otherwise good, later generations perverted, when they made it a fixed law of one communion in the year. The result is that almost everyone, once they have communicated, sleep on secure, as if they were free of all obligation for the rest of the year. It ought to have been far otherwise. At least each week the table of the Lord ought to have been spread for the company of Christians, and the promises declared on which we might then spiritually feed. No one, indeed, ought to be forced, but all ought to be exhorted and stirred up; and the dullness of the sluggish ought also to be rebuked, so that all, like people starving, should come to the feast.

It was not without cause, then, that I complained at the outset that this practice had been introduced by the cunning of the devil, a practice which, by prescribing one day in the year, makes the whole year a year of laziness. We can see, indeed, that this corrupt abuse had already crept in by the time of Chrysostom; but at the same time we can also see how much it displeased him. For he complains in bitter terms, in the passage I quoted just now, that there was so great an inequality in this matter, that they did not approach often, at other times of the year, even when prepared, but only at Easter, though unprepared. Then he exclaims: "O custom! O presumption! In vain, then, is the daily offering made; in vain do we stand at the altar. There is no one who partakes along with us." So far is he from having approved the practice by lending his authority to it.

From the same forge came another decree, which snatched, or rather robbed, half of the Supper from the greater part of the people of God, namely, the symbol of the blood. Forbidden to the laity and the profane (such are the titles they give to God's heritage), it became the special possession of a few shaven and anointed individuals. The decree of the eternal God is that all are to drink. An upstart dares to make this obsolete and to abolish it by a new and contrary law, proclaiming that all are not to drink. And so that such lawmakers may not seem to fight against their God without any reason, they make a pretext of the dangers that might happen if the sacred cup were given to all without distinction, as if these dangers had not been foreseen and provided for by the eternal wisdom of God.

Then they reason cleverly, so they suppose, that the one is enough for the two. For if the body is, as they say, the whole Christ, who cannot be separated from his body, then the blood is included with the body by concomitance. Here we see how far our human sense falls in step with God whenever, to any degree at all, it begins to rage and run wild with the reins loosened. The Lord, pointing to the bread, says, "This is my body." Then, pointing to the cup, he calls it his blood. The audacity of human reason objects and says: the bread is the blood, the wine is the body, as if the Lord had distinguished his body from his blood, both by words and by signs, for no reason, and as if it had ever been heard that the body of Christ, or his blood, is called both God and man. Certainly, if he had meant to designate himself wholly, he might have said, "It is I," according to the way Scripture speaks, and not, "This is my body," "This is my blood." But wishing to help the weakness of our faith, he set the cup apart from the bread, to show that he is no less sufficient as drink than as food.

Now, if one part is taken away, we can find only half of the elements in what remains. Therefore, even if it were true, as they pretend, that the blood is in the bread, and, on the other hand, the body in the cup, by concomitance, yet they deprive godly people of that confirmation of faith which Christ delivered as necessary. Bidding farewell, then, to their subtleties, let us hold fast to the benefit that, by the ordinance of Christ, is obtained through a double pledge.

I am well aware, indeed, how the ministers of Satan, whose usual practice is to hold the Scriptures in scorn, raise their objections here. See Calvin, On the Lord's Supper; also, Against the Theologians of Paris; also, The True Method of Reforming the Church.

But why argue about a fact that is perfectly well known? Look at all the Greek and Latin writers. Passages of the same kind appear everywhere. Nor did this practice fall out of use as long as there was one particle of integrity in the Church. Gregory, whom you may justly call the last bishop of Rome, says that it was still observed in his own age.

Third, why did our Savior say of the bread simply, "Take, eat," but of the cup, "Drink of it, all of you," as if he had deliberately intended to guard against the cunning of Satan? Fourth, if, as they will have it, the Lord honored only priests with his Supper, what man would ever have dared to call to it strangers whom the Lord had excluded, and to give them a share in a gift that was not in his own power to give, without any command from the one who alone could give it? Indeed, what presumption do they show in our own day in distributing the symbol of Christ's body to the common people, if they have no command or example from the Lord?

Fifth, did Paul lie when he said to the Corinthians, "I received from the Lord that which I also delivered to you" (1 Cor. 11:23)? What he delivered, he afterward declares to be this: that all should share in both symbols without distinction. But if Paul received from the Lord that all were to be admitted without distinction, let those who drive away almost the whole people of God consider from whom they have received their practice, since they cannot now pretend to have their authority from God, with whom there is no "yes and no" (2 Cor. 1:19, 20). And yet they dare to cloak these abominations with the name of the Church, and defend them under that pretext, as if those antichrists were the Church, who so recklessly trample under foot, lay waste, and abolish the teaching and the ordinances of Christ; or as if the apostolic Church, in which religion flourished in full vigor, were not the Church.
